questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-2,4,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,4,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(-2){e}^{0}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-2,0,-2).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}$ at the point $(1,9,4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$

questions.problem: At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$
